abstract: Previously, animal breeding prioritized enhancing key economic traits to improve production efficiency, leading to a gradual difference in meat quality. However, the genetic factors influencing meat quality remain unclear. To identify key genetic pathways contributing to meat quality, native Chinese yellow-feathered chicken (Qingyuan Partridge Chicken, QPC; female, n=10), and commercial chicken broiler (Cobb broiler, CB; female, n=10) were used for meat quality assessment through metabolomics, proteomics, and phosphoproteomics sequencing. The results show that QPC had lower pH (93.12%), shear force (81.46%), cooking loss (69.29%), moisture content (93.24%) and muscle fiber area (46.04%), but higher meat color values (a*(163.65%) and b*(250.27%)), drip loss (146.32%), and intramuscular fat content (382.01%) than CB ( p < 0.05). Metabolomic, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic analyses were jointly conducted, revealing significant differences in energy metabolism strategies. Higher glycolytic enzyme activity was observed in QPC (ENO1, GAPDH, GPI, PFKM, PKM, and TPI1, p < 0.05), while more energetic phosphate compounds were stored in CB. CB had higher Na + /K + Pump protein abundance (SCN4A, LOC107051305, ATP1B4, ATP12A, ATP1A1, and ATP1A2, p < 0.05) and phosphorylation (ATP1A2-Ser662, p < 0.05) and Ca 2+ channel protein abundance (ATP2B4, SRL, CACNB1, CACNA1S, CACNA2D1, CAMK2G, LOC107050717 and TNNC2, p < 0.05) than QPC. In QPC, CAMKII autophosphorylation activated downstream protein and increased Ca 2+ . These results suggest CB is more contractile than QPC, contributing to meat quality between CB and QPC.

Materials and methods
Animal and sample information
All animal experimental procedures in this study complied with the requirements of the Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee of South China Agricultural University (No. 2023f273). Qingyuan Partridge Chicken (QPC, n=10) was provided by Fengxiang Partridge Development Co. Ltd, Qingyuan City, Guangdong Province, China, and Cobb Broiler (CB, n=10) was provided by Nanhai Breeding Poultry Co. Ltd, Foshan City, Guangdong Province, China.
All experimental animals were female to ensure consistency and reliability in evaluating meat quality. All chickens were housed individually in single cages, with free access to feed and water. The broilers were reared and managed following guidelines (GB/T 5916-2020, NY/T 1871-2010). The hens were slaughtered at their respective market ages: 40 days for CB and 120 days for QPC.
Slaughter procedures adhered to the national standard of China (GB/T 19478-2018). All chickens are transported by truck to the slaughterhouse and fasted for 12 hours with free access to water. Chickens were stunned by electric shock until unconscious and immediately slaughtered by cutting the cervical artery and jugular vein to ensure effective bleeding within 3 min. Breast muscles were collected from a uniform anatomical position across all individuals, then stored in liquid nitrogen. Six samples from each group were randomly selected for metabolomic, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic analyses. For histological examination, breast muscles were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and prepared for hematoxylin and eosin staining. Meat quality measurements were taken immediately after muscle collection.
Measurement of meat quality traits
Various measurements were conducted to assess meat quality, including pH, meat color (a*, b*, L*), shear force, cooking loss, moisture content, intramuscular fat content, and muscle fiber area. Five samples each of moisture content, intramuscular fat, and muscle fiber area were randomly selected for measurement, with each sample being measured twice. Conversely, all ten samples of pH, meat color, shear force, and cooking loss were selected for measurement, with each sample measured thrice, and the average value is taken. The assessment of meat quality parameters followed the methodology outlined by Chen (
Chen et al., 2024
). pH was determined using a pH meter (DELTA 320, Mettler Toledo, Columbus, OH, USA) at three different locations on the breast muscle, calibrated with standard pH 4.0 and pH 7.0 buffers before measurement. Meat color was quantified using a 3NH - NH310 colorimeter (3NH, Guangzhou, China), with three replicates for each sample. In this measurement, positive to negative a* values indicated a color change from red to green, positive to negative b* values indicated a color change from yellow to blue, and high to low L* values indicated a color change from light to dark.
The breast muscles were sliced into 2 × 1 × 3 cm³ cubes for shear force, drip loss and cooking loss analyses. Shear force was measured using a digital tenderness meter (C-LM4, Tenovo, Beijing, China) at 200 mm/min, with the section perpendicular to the muscle fiber direction. Drip loss (%) was calculated as the weight loss percentage after suspending in sealed bags stored at 4°C for 24 hours. Cooking loss was determined by the weight difference before and after cooking in a water bath at 85°C until 80°C internal temperature. Intramuscular fat (IMF) content was measured using a Soxtec extraction auto analyzer (Soxtec™ 2050, FOSS Analytical, Hillerod, Denmark). IMF content was determined based on the Soxhlet extraction method in nation standard for the determination of fat in food (GB/5009.6-2016). In short, after removing all the fascia from fresh meat, it is dried and ground into fine particles. The fat is extracted using anhydrous ether in a Soxtec extraction auto analyzer, followed by evaporation of the solvent and subsequent drying. Moisture content was determined by the weight difference between dried and fresh meat. The Hematoxylin and Eosin staining and imaging were performed by Wuhan Pinuofei Biological Technology Company, and the muscle fiber area was quantified using ImageJ software.
Metabolomics detection and data processing
A measured quantity of the sample was weighed into a 2 mL centrifuge tube. Then, 1000 µL of tissue extract consisting of 75% methanol (9:1 chloroform) and 25% H
2
O (Fisher Scientific, Loughborough, UK) was added. Steel balls were then introduced, and the mixture was ground in a tissue grinder (MB-96, Meibi, China) at 50 Hz for 60 s, repeated twice. The solution was sonicated for 30 min (KQ-800DE, Shumei, China), left on ice for 30 min, and centrifuged (H1850-R, Xiangyi, China) for 10 min at 12,000 rpm at 4°C. The supernatant was collected, transferred to a new 2 mL centrifuge tube, concentrated, and dried (5305 Eppendorf, USA). Then, the samples were re-dissolved in 200 µL of a 50% acetonitrile solution containing 2-chloro-1-phenylalanine (4 ppm) (Aladdin, Shanghai, China). The resulting supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and transferred to a detection vial for LC-MS analysis.
For chromatographic separation, a Thermo Vanquish (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) UHPLC system with an ACQUITY UPLC® HSS T3 column (2.1 × 150 mm, 1.8 μm) (Waters, Milford, MA, USA) was used at a flow rate of 0.25 mL/min. The mobile phases were 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid in water for positive ion mode. In negative ion mode, the mobile phases were acetonitrile and 5 mM ammonium formate water and the scheduled program is carried out.
Data was collected using a Thermo Orbitrap Exploris 120 mass spectrometry detector (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) with an electrospray ion source. The positive ion spray voltage was 3.50 kV, while the negative ion spray voltage was -2.50 kV. The sheath gas and auxiliary gas were maintained at 30 arb and 10 arb, respectively. The capillary temperature was 325 °C. Primary full scans were performed at a resolution of 60,000, covering a scan range of m/z 100-1000, and the secondary cleavage was performed using an HCD with a collision energy of 30% and a secondary resolution of 15,000. Four ions were fragmented prior to signal acquisition, while dynamic exclusion was implemented to filter out unnecessary MS/MS information.
The raw mass spectrometry files were converted to mzXML format using the MSConvert tool in the Proteowizard. Data processing was performed in R 4.2.3. Peak detection, filtering, and alignment were completed using the XCMS package (bw = 2, ppm = 15, peakwidth = c(5, 30), mzwid = 0.015, mzdiff = 0.01, and method = "centWave"). Public databases HMDB, massbank, LipidMaps, mzcloud, and KEGG were utilized for subfstance identification. Data correction was achieved using the LOESS signal correction method based on QC samples. Substances with RSD > 30% in the QC samples were filtered out. Statistical testing (
t
-test) was used to calculate the
p
value. Metabolites were considered statistically significant by p value (
p
< 0.05).
Protein detection and data processing
The samples were ground with liquid nitrogen and mixed with lysis buffer (lysate: protease inhibitor 50:1), vortexed then ultrasonicated. Centrifugation (Eppendorf, Germany) at 14,000g for 20 minutes, the supernatant collected. Protein aliquots incubated with 5mM DTT (Amresco, USA) at 37°C for 1 hour, then 10 mM iodoacetamide (Amresco, USA) added at room temperature for 45 minutes. The sample was diluted 4 times with 25mM ammonium bicarbonate (Sigma-Aldrich, USA), trypsin (Promega, USA) added at a ratio of 50:1 and incubated at 37°C overnight. The next day, formic acid (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) added to adjust pH to less than 3 to halt digestion. Desalting the samples using a C18 desalting column, activated with 100% acetonitrile (J.T. Baker, USA) and equilibrated with 0.1% formic acid. The sample loaded, washed with 0.1% formic acid and eluted with 70% acetonitrile. The eluate collected and flow-through solution lyophilized.
Tandem Mass Tags (TMT) (Thermo fisher, USA) reagent was thawed at room temperature, 41 μl of acetonitrile added, and mixed by shaking for 5 min followed by centrifugation. The TMT reagent was added to 100 μg of the digested sample and allowed to react at room temperature for 1 h. Reaction was terminated by adding ammonia. The labeled samples were pooled, vortexed, shaken, and centrifuged to collect the precipitate. The samples were dried by vacuum freeze-drying using a vacuum centrifugal concentrator (Jiaimu, China). The dried samples were re-dissolved in 100 μl of mobile phase A and centrifuged at 14,000g for 20 min. The supernatant was collected and subjected to high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).
Mobile phases Liquid A (100% H
2
O, 0.1% formic acid) and Liquid B (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) were prepared. The lyophilized powder was dissolved in 10 μL of Liquid A. The sample was centrifuged at 14,000 g for 20 min at 4 °C. The RIGOL L-3000 liquid chromatography system (Rigol, China) was used for liquid chromatographic elution. Separation was performed using an ORBITRAP ECLIPSE mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, USA) and generated raw data of mass spectrometry (.raw). In this study, the Gallus gallus database was Gallus_gallus_uniprot_20230307.
This experiment used two criteria for protein filtering: (1) unique peptide ≥1 and (2) quantification in at least 50% of samples. Protein quantification values were normalized using the median method and missing values were filled using the K-Nearest Neighbors algorithm. A
t
-test assessed the statistical significance of differences in protein quantification values between groups. The
p
value value is corrected using the BH FDR.
Phosphorylation site assay
Samples underwent lysis and protein extraction using SDT buffer (4% SDS, 100 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM DTT, pH 7.6). Protein content was quantified using a BCA protein assay kit (Bio-Rad, USA). Protein digestion was conducted with trypsin following the filter-assisted sample preparation (FASP) protocol. Digested peptides from each sample were desalted using C18 cartridges (Sigma, USA), concentrated by vacuum centrifugation, and reconstituted in 40 µl of 0.1% (v/v) formic acid. Phosphopeptides were enriched using the High-SelectTM Fe-NTA Phosphopeptides Enrichment Kit (Thermo Scientific, USA). Enriched phosphopeptides were lyophilized and resuspended in 20 µl of upsampling buffer containing 0.1% formic acid.
LC-MS/MS analysis was performed on a timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer (Bruker, USA) coupled to a Nanoelute (Bruker Daltonics, USA) for 60 min. Peptides were loaded onto a C18 reversed-phase analytical column (homemade, 25 cm × 75 μm, 1.9 μm, C18) in buffer A (0.1% formic acid) and separated in buffer B (84% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid) using a linear gradient at 300 nl/min. The mass spectrometer operated in positive ion mode, collecting ion mobility mass spectra from m/z 100-1700 with 1/k0 of 0.6-1.6, followed by 10 cycles of PASEF MS/MS with target intensity of 1.5 k and threshold of 2500. Active exclusion was enabled with release time of 0.4 minutes. The MS raw data for each sample were combined and analyzed for identification and quantitative analysis using MaxQuant software. The database was uniprot_Gallus_70746_20230111. Data processing was performed in R 4.2.2. The quantitative information of the target protein set is normalized to a range of -1 to 1.
The MeMe suite was utilized to predict potential conserved motifs, and protein domain analysis was conducted using the Pfam database. The Blast2GO tool was employed to annotate the GO terms. KEGG pathway annotation for the target protein set was performed using the KAAS (KEGG Automatic Annotation Server) software. Direct and indirect interaction relationships among the target proteins were identified through the STRING database (
http://string-db.org/
), and the interaction network was generated and analyzed using the Cytoscape software.
Statistical analysis
In this study, each meat quality parameter was measured at least three times, with the average value is taken. An independent samples
t
-test was used to compare two groups, with significance determined at
p
< 0.05.

Introduction
Poultry meat is an important agricultural product, and according to OECD-FAO, it is projected to account for 41% of total global meat protein by 2030, with 17.8% higher in consumption than 2022 and a shift to poultry meat consumption (
OECD and Nations, 2021
). Poultry has advantages of high feed conversion, low fecal emissions, affordable price, and wide consumer groups. Qingyuan Partridge Chicken (QPC) is a premium Chinese local breed in Qingyuan City, Guangdong Province, China. It is a quality broiler with tender meat and unique flavor, well-liked by Chinese consumers, but has disadvantages of a long feeding cycle and low meat production efficiency. The Cobb Broiler (CB) is an excellent commercial breed with recognized production performance. Poultry breeders aim to increase yield and improve meat quality. Therefore, understanding scientific basis of meat quality differences between local slow-type and commercial fast-type chickens is necessary to enhance chicken meat quality, production performance, and meet consumer demand.
For consumers, poultry meat's intuitive quality is mainly color, taste, and possibly fat content. For the producer, meat quality encompasses a combination of quality and homogeneity in terms of pH, water holding capacity, cooking loss, tenderness, and muscle fibers count, among others (
Zhang et al., 2020
). The main factors affecting meat quality include genetics, age, feeding management, and environment, with genetics being the most fundamental factor affecting meat quality. Estimates of heritability for meat quality traits in broilers were very high (0.35-0.81), making genetic selection the best tool for improving meat quality (
Mir et al., 2017
). The leading indicators of meat quality are color, tenderness, flavor, juiciness, and water holding capacity. All meat quality indicators are interrelated and do not work individually but result from a combination of metabolic and structural factors in the meat. Meat metabolism, such as glycolysis, affects meat's pH, color, and intramuscular fat content and indirectly affects juiciness and water retention (
Fletcher, 2002
). Similarly, the fiber structure and composition of the meat also affect tenderness, juiciness, and color (
Dransfield and Sosnicki, 1999
).
Metabolomics, proteomics, and phosphoproteomics are valuable tools for analyzing complex biochemical pathways involved in meat quality. Metabolomics, a powerful tool, helps to identify the types and quantities of metabolites to elucidate metabolic processes. It has broad applications for identifying and analyzing meat composition, widely used in meat quality studies. For instance, beef pH and color changes result from upregulation of tricarboxylic acid cycle metabolites and increased mitochondrial content, and downregulated glycolytic metabolites and glycogen-degrading enzymes. Conversely, lamb color stability correlates with myoglobin chemistry and antioxidant activity-related metabolites (
Zhang et al., 2021
).
Proteomics has been widely used to unravel complex biological mechanisms underlying meat quality and identify potential biomarkers. Studies have identified actin, myosin, alpha-1,4-glucan phosphorylase, phosphoglucomutase 1, heat shock protein beta-1, tubulin beta-7 chain, and skeletal muscle type tropomodulin (fragment) as marker proteins associated with meat quality degradation in prepared chicken breast and can be used to evaluate the chicken breast meat quality (
Luo et al., 2021
).
Phosphorylation is the most widespread and important form of regulatory modification in protein post-translational modification and plays an important regulatory role in metabolic processes through protein kinase and phosphatases. Phosphoproteomics can identify phosphorylation sites on protein sequences and content analysis and serves as a vital tool in meat quality research. Studies have found that in broilers, SLC7A5 at Ser21, MRC2 at Ser1359, CRAT at Ser341, and AUP1 at Ser377 positively impact protein and intramuscular fat deposition (
Weng et al., 2022
).
This study hypothesizes that local slow-type chickens and commercial fast-type broilers have significantly different meat quality due to genetic differences. Therefore, we analyzed the breast muscles of both breeds using metabolomic, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic techniques to identify genetic differences related to meat quality. Multi-omics integration can systematically elucidate the genetic metabolic network responsible for meat quality differences. This study aimed to understand the genetic determinants contributing to variations in meat quality between Chinese local chickens and commercial fast-type broilers.

Result
Analysis of differences in meat quality traits between QPC and CB
To reveal meat quality differences between QPC and CB breast muscles, we evaluated representative meat characteristics. Physical characteristics of the breast muscles from both breeds were measured, revealing the significantly higher pH in CB compared to QPC (
Fig. 1
B). Meat color assessment showed no significant difference in L* values between the two breeds but QPC exhibited significantly higher a* and b* values than CB (
Fig. 1
C), indicating that the flesh color of QPC's breast muscles was reddish and that of CB was more pallid. The drip loss of the breast muscle was significantly higher in QPC than in CB (
Fig. 1
D). Both cooking loss and moisture content were significantly higher in CB than in QPC (
Fig. 1
D). The intramuscular fat content of QPC was much greater than that of CB and shear force was significantly lower in QPC than in CB (
Fig. 1
D). Additionally, the muscle fibers area was significantly higher in CB than in QPC (
Fig. 1
D). In short, there is significant meat quality difference between QPC and CB, with QPC exhibiting lower pH, shear force, cooking loss, moisture content, and muscle fibers area, and higher meat color values, drip loss, and intramuscular fat content compared to CB.

Based on MS/MS fragmentation patterns, 324 metabolites were annotated and classified into 13 groups (
Fig. 2
A). All metabolites clustering is shown in
Fig. 2
B. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of 324 metabolites revealed distinct separation between two breeds (
Fig. 2
C). Among 324 metabolites, 26 were up-regulated, and 38 were down-regulated in QPC versus CB. We performed a KEGG enrichment analysis of differential metabolites (Supplementary A.1B). Exploring variances in meat quality between QPC and CB by multi-omics analysis
Metabolomics, proteomics, and phosphoproteomics have been used to explore poultry meat quality differentiation. However, the overall mechanisms by which genetic differences between breeds affect meat quality remain largely unknown. Metabolomic analysis revealed significant variance in metabolic profiles of QPC and CB, particularly in amino acid and energy metabolism pathways. ATP content in QPC breast muscle was 1.912-fold higher than CB (but not significant), while ADP and AMP contents were nearly equivalent. Moreover, while phosphocreatine remained consistent, sodium creatine phosphate dibasic tetrahydrate and creatine concentrations were significantly higher in CB. Additionally, no significant difference in abundance was observed for NAD
+
and NADH in oxidative phosphorylation. In summary, CB stores more high-energy phosphates than QPC.
Proteins and proteins with significantly different phosphorylation intensities were classified into three groups: myofiber-associated, glycolytic, and kinase/phosphorylase (Supplementary A.6, Supplementary A.7). Among significantly different glycolysis-related proteins, all were higher in QPC than CB, except for FBP2. Within glycolysis-related enzymes, ENO1, GAPDH, GPI, PFKM, PKM, and TPI1 showed higher phosphorylation in QPC than CB, while GYG1 and PGAM1 had opposite trends. In the TCA cycle and glycogen metabolism, only CKM, implicated in creatine metabolism, showed significantly higher abundance in QPC. Notably, the ATP synthase family and SLC25A6 were less abundant in QPC than CB (except for ATP5F1AZ, ATP5B, and ATP5J2), with similar fold change differences. Among kinases and phosphatases, PRKCA, PHKA, PPP1R3A, and PPP1CA had higher phosphorylation in QPC than CB. Additionally, CKM had significantly higher phosphorylation intensity at Ser164 and Ser337 in QPC (2.541 and 1.689 times), with phosphorylation at Ser158 only observed in QPC. The ATP produced by glycolysis elicits an activation response in creatine kinase. Notably, while protein abundance showed no difference between breeds, the phosphorylation intensity of PRKCA at Thr499 was significantly higher in QPC than CB, with phosphorylation at Ser149 only detected in QPC. This reflects CB's relatively higher demand and capacity for ATP synthesis. In summary, QPC and CB have different energy metabolism strategies. QPC favors rapid ATP acquisition through glycolysis, with excess ATP activating creatine kinase for small amounts of phosphocreatine storage. CB stores more high-energy phosphates and releases ATP rapidly through high-energy phosphates when needed. Under differing energy metabolism strategies, QPC promotes glycolysis, generates more lactic acid, and lowers the pH of the breast muscle. These differences in energy metabolism strategy led to variation in meat quality between QPC and CB.
In the CB, proteins abundances associated with Na
+
/K
+
transport were higher than in QPC, including SCN4A, LOC107051305, ATP1B4, ATP12A, ATP1A1, and ATP1A2. Furthermore, the phosphorylation intensity of the ATP1A2 protein at Ser662 was significantly higher in CB than QPC. The higher levels of Na
+
/K
+
pump protein abundance and phosphorylation observed in CB indicate more frequently membrane potential regulation, suggesting greater muscle contraction intensity than QPC.
In QPC, ATP2B4 protein abundance was significantly lower than CB. SRL, CACNB1, CACNA1S, CACNA2D1, CAMK2G, LOC107050717 and TNNC2 were significantly more abundant in CB. CACNA1S, ATP2B4, RYR3, TNNT3, and CACNB1 showed higher phosphorylation intensity in CB. ATP2B4, a calcium-transporting ATPase, catalyzes the transfer of the phosphate group of ATPs to ATPase, altering its conformation to enable active transport of Ca
2+
, playing a critical role in intracellular calcium homeostasis. RYR3 is one of the isoforms of RYR and functions as a mediator of Ca
2+
release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum/endoplasmic reticulum membrane. Ca
2+
plays a pivotal role in myofilament gliding during muscle contraction. Hence, calcium metabolism appears to be more intense in CB than QPC, suggesting that muscle fibers in CB contract with greater intensity than in QPC.
MYLK2 was phosphorylated only in QPC. CAMKII kinase phosphorylation intensity was higher in QPC than CB. MYLK2 plays a critical role in skeletal muscle contraction, activated by Ca
2+
and phosphorylation-activated CAMKII. Previous results showed the Ca
2+
transport metabolic strength is higher in CB than QPC. Here in QPC, CAMKII could activate its own catalytic activity through autophosphorylation to increase Ca
2+
sensitivity and enhance muscle contraction. Additionally, in CB, Titin and Nebulin have significantly higher protein abundance than QPC. Titin and Nebulin play important roles in myofiber function. CB's muscle fibers are likely to be more active than those in QPC.
In conclusion, the results of metabolomics, proteomics, and phosphoproteomics suggest that CB has a greater muscle contractile capacity than QPC across four key aspects: ATP levels, myofiber electrical signals, Ca
2+
regulation, and sarcomere protein abundance and regulation (
Fig. 5
). This heightened contractile capacity is a key factor in initiating muscle hypertrophy, aligning with the higher meat production efficiency of CB, a commercial broiler breed, versus QPC, a local China native chicken.

Discussion
pH is an important indicator of meat quality, typically falling within the range of 5.8-5.9 for chicken breast muscle, and either too high or too low will affect the quality of the meat (
Bihan-Duval et al., 2018
). An excessively high pH can cause the meat to have an abnormal flavor when boiled (
Korkeala et al., 1988
). Moreover, if the meat is dark, firm, and dry (DFD), it will also present higher pH and moisture content (
Guàrdia et al., 2010
). Studies have shown that high pH meat is suitable for processed products, while low pH meat is suitable for handling with ingredients (
Chan et al., 2011
). This aligns with CB's commercial suitability for further processing and QPC's suitability for simpler cooking methods like steaming and boiling. Meat color significantly influences consumer acceptance, as excessively pale or dark meat can impact consumer preference (
de Araújo et al., 2022
). Differences in color are primarily attributed to proteins, pigment types, and redox reactions factor variations in the muscle (
Hughes et al., 2020
). This suggests that meat quality differences between breeds may relate to protein composition variations. Drip loss measures fresh meat's water retention capacity, directly influenced by factors such as pH, ionic strength, protein hydrolysis, and oxidation (
Huff-Lonergan and Lonergan, 2005
,
Logan et al., 2019
). Cooking loss indicates meat's ability to hold water at high temperatures, and juiciness can be predicted from cooking loss (
Tan et al., 2022
). Water content can influence color, pH, flavor, and tissue status, and importantly, the immobile water in meat is critical for juiciness (
Qiao et al., 2001
). QPC has more intramuscular fat than CB. Intramuscular fat is a significant factor influencing the flavor of meat and can affect tenderness and juiciness of cooked meat (
Wood et al., 2008
). Shear force is a key determinant of tenderness (
Kerth and Kerth, 2013
). Fiber area, diameter, and number impact meat quality, with fiber diameter correlating with tenderness (
Klont et al., 1998
).
Creatine is essential for muscle energy metabolism, interacting with ATP to convert into phosphocreatine for energy storage, which balances ATP levels in the brain and muscle. The creatine/phosphocreatine system is essential for energy metabolism, promoting muscle mass increase, and preventing muscle atrophy (
Kazak and Cohen, 2020
,
Sun et al., 2022
). In chickens, dietary supplementation with creatine enhances the 24-hour pH value of the pectoralis major muscle, reduces drip loss, improves muscle energy status, enhances meat quality, and alleviates the rapid muscle glycolysis and meat quality decline induced by transport (
Duan et al., 2022
,
Zhang et al., 2017
). Creatine also promotes protein synthesis under normal conditions and, during starvation, mitigates muscle atrophy by inhibiting catabolism and enhancing mitochondrial function (
Kazak and Cohen, 2020
). It is known that CB has a significantly higher growth rate than QPC. Therefore, this may be one of the reasons for the higher creatine content in CB. Additionally, studies have shown that Medium-chain monoglycerides (MG) dietary supplementation improves the quality of chicken broth and fresh meat quality, and KEGG analysis revealed that amino acid metabolic pathways such as histidine metabolism, phenylalanine metabolism, and pyruvate metabolism are associated with enhanced meat quality, composition, and taste in broilers (
Liu et al., 2021
). In the KEGG results of this study, histidine and phenylalanine metabolic pathways were enriched, indicating these pathways also contributing factors to the differences in meat quality differences between QPC and CB. In summary, the metabolomic results suggest that QPC and CB exhibit distinct metabolic landscapes, with creatine as a significant differential metabolite and amino acid metabolism as a key pathway of metabolic differences, both critical factors affecting meat quality.
MYH1 is a component of thick myofilaments in type II muscle fibers. TNNC1 is a centrally regulated protein in striated muscle and is located on actin filaments with tropomyosin. In chicken, MYH1 is identified as a marker of meat freshness (
Luo et al., 2021
). In beef, MYH1 was associated with marbling values of longissimus thoracis and semimembranosus muscles, while TNNC1 was significantly associated with tenderness, and MYH1 and TNNC1 are regarded as related proteins affecting shear force and intramuscular fat (
Bonnet et al., 2020
,
Gagaoua et al., 2020
). MYBPC binds to actin and is an essential regulator of sarcomere contraction through its phosphorylation state (
Robinett et al., 2019
). Thus, proteomic results suggest differential protein abundance is a reason for meat quality differences between QPC and CB.
The results of this study revealed significantly higher phosphorylation levels of glycolytic enzymes, AGL, ALDH1A1, ENO1, and PKM in QPC compared to CB or exclusive phosphorylation sites in QPC. In contrast, phosphorylation modification of glycogen synthase was only found in CB. Studies have indicated that differential phosphorylation of proteins in muscle contraction and various energy metabolism pathways affects the final pH of beef, while phosphorylation of glycogen synthase can influence the process of pH drop in muscle-to-meat conversion, and thus meat tenderness by regulating glycogen synthesis and catabolism (
Li et al., 2023
). Higher levels of glycolysis produce more lactic acid, suggesting that phosphorylation of glycolysis-related proteins contributes to pH and meat quality differences between QPC and CB. Weng, et al. (
Weng et al., 2022
) found that up-regulated phosphorylated proteins resulted in larger fibers, contributing to reduced pressing loss and tenderness; in contrast, lower levels of phosphorylated glycolytic enzymes, phosphorylase kinases, and calcium-associated proteins reduce the acidity of the meat. Phosphorylation of muscle fibers is one of the crucial influences on tenderness in beef and lamb. Chen, et al. (
Chen et al., 2019
) indicate that sarcomere function-associated proteins in tough meat were significantly higher than those in tender meat at different times, with myofibrillar proteins (e.g., myosin light chain 2 and actin) being particularly pronounced. Myofiber-related proteins such as TINI2, TPM2, MYOZ2, MYH1G, MTMR3, MYH1F, RYR3, MYLK2, and MYLK4 exhibited significantly higher phosphorylation levels in CB compared to QPC, suggesting that the different phosphorylation abundances of myofiber-associated proteins contribute to meat quality differences between QPC and CB and results in higher shear force, cooking loss, and lower drip loss for CB compared to QPC. In summary, differential phosphorylation of muscle fiber and glycolytic proteins is a significant factor influencing meat quality differences between breeds.
ATP serves as a prototypical high-energy phosphate compound and its hydrolysis releases large amounts of energy, functioning as a cellular energy carrier. Phosphorylation enhances glycolytic enzyme activity, promoting glycolysis and regulating lactic acid and PH (
Li et al., 2023
). Additionally, CKM, a creatine kinase isoenzyme, catalyzes the reversible conversion of creatine and ATP to phosphocreatine and ADP, a critical process for muscle energy metabolism. Phosphorylation can enhance CKM catalytic activity (
Lin et al., 2009
). PRKCA is a multifunctional enzyme that regulates downstream protein phosphorylation and controls its activity via self-phosphorylation (
Newton, 1995
). CKM is one of PRKCA's substrates (
Abnous and Storey, 2007
). This indicates that QPC responds to higher ATP levels, activating creatine metabolism to store energy.
In skeletal muscle, excitation triggers transmembrane ions flow, namely K
+
efflux and Na
+
influx across the cell membrane. Following action potential disappearance, the Na
+
/K
+
pump actively transports Na
+
to the extracellular and pumps K
+
back into the intracellular, maintaining normal homeostasis, its primary function. Under physiological conditions, Na
+
/K
+
-ATPase catalyzes the transfer of ATP's terminal phosphate group to Na
+
/K
+
-ATPase's amino acid residues in the presence of Na
+
and Mg
2+
. Phosphorylation of ATPase leads to conformational changes in the enzyme and promotes Na
+
binding to Na
+
/K
+
-ATPase and its transport to the outside of the cell. Hence, adequate Na
+
/K
+
pump activity and capacity are crucial, regulated by both rapid activation and long-term adjustments in pump content or capacity. Studies show higher-intensity contractions upregulate Na
+
/K
+
pump content in skeletal muscle (
Clausen, 2003
). These reflect the membrane potential regulation process occurs more frequently in CB, indicating greater muscle contraction intensity than QPC.
RYR3 phosphorylation can promote Ca
2+
release (
Meissner, 2017
). During excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle, calcium ions are released into the sarcoplasm through the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)/endoplasmic reticulum in response to the depolarization of the outer fiber membrane. Ca
2+
then diffuses into the thin filaments and binds to Ca
2+
regulatory sites on troponin to activate muscle contraction (
Baylor and Hollingworth, 2011
). Thus, Ca
2+
plays a pivotal role in myofilament gliding during muscle contraction. Calcium metabolism was higher intensity in CB compared to QPC, indicating that muscle fibers in CB contract with greater intensity than in QPC.
MYLK2 plays a critical role in skeletal muscle contraction, activation of which is triggered by Ca
2+
and phosphorylation-activated CAMKII. This activation can lead to phosphorylation of the myosin light chain kinase (MYLC), increasing myosin regulatory light chain (RLC) sensitivity to Ca
2+
and enhancing muscle contraction (
Zhi et al., 2005
). In QPC, CAMKII activates its own catalytic activity through autophosphorylation. CAMKII phosphorylates and activates MLCK, which in turn phosphorylates and activates RLC to increase Ca
2+
sensitivity and enhance muscle contraction.
Conclusion
This study elucidates molecular mechanisms underlying meat quality differences between QPC and CB chicken breeds. QPC has higher glycolytic enzyme activity, while CB has more high-energy phosphate storage. Additionally, CB has superior muscle contractility due to higher Na
+
/K
+
pump and Ca
2+
channel abundance and phosphorylation. In summary, QPC and CB have different contractile capabilities and energy metabolism strategies in breast muscles, contributing to meat quality differences.
